questions.lesson_line: Volume is today's trading. Open interest only grows when both sides open.

wrong.Volume 300; open interest rises to 1,500: Open interest rises only when both sides open. The seller was closing.
wrong.Volume 600; open interest up to 1,500: Volume counts contracts traded, and 300 changed hands. Open interest didn't rise either.
wrong.No volume; open interest 900: There was a trade, so there's volume. Open interest falls only when both sides close.

questions.story: You buy calls the day before earnings. The report is good and the stock opens up 2%. Your calls open lower than you paid.
questions.q: What most likely hurt your calls?
choices: Implied volatility fell after the report
Delta flipped negative on the gap
questions.answer: Implied volatility fell after the report
questions.why: Implied volatility fell after the report. It can be bid up before earnings and often drops sharply once the news is out. That can outweigh a small move your way.
questions.lesson_line: Before earnings you pay for the expected move. If the stock moves less, the premium shrinks.

wrong.Delta flipped negative on the gap: A call's delta stays between 0 and 1. It doesn't turn negative.
wrong.Your calls were assigned overnight: Only writers get assigned. You own the calls.
wrong.Open interest dropped overnight: Open interest doesn't set the price. It counts open contracts.

questions.story: Before earnings, your platform shows an expected move of $8 on a $100 stock.
questions.q: What does that $8 tell you?
choices: The size of move priced in, either way
The stock is expected to rise $8
Your max loss if you hold the stock
questions.answer: The size of move priced in, either way
questions.why: The size of move priced in, either way. It's an estimate of magnitude from option prices, with no direction and no guarantee.
questions.lesson_line: Use the expected move to size your risk into earnings, not to pick a side.

wrong.It will close between $92 and $108: It's not a promise. The stock can move more or less than what's priced in.
wrong.The stock is expected to rise $8: An expected move has no direction. It covers a move up or down.
wrong.Your max loss if you hold the stock: The stock can move past it. The expected move doesn't cap your loss on shares.

questions.q: A 0DTE option is a special contract the exchange lists on the morning it expires.
questions.why: False. 0DTE just means zero days to expiration. It's a listed option that has reached its last day, and it's rarely listed that morning.
questions.lesson_line: Every option is 0DTE on its last day. Time decay is fastest at the end.

questions.story: You're scanning calls for a cheap swing trade. The 0.10-delta call costs $0.15 and looks like a bargain.
questions.q: Read as a rough probability, what does that delta suggest?
choices: About a 10% chance it ends in the money
It gains $10 for each $1 the stock rises
It loses 10% of its value each day
It is 10% out of the money
questions.answer: About a 10% chance it ends in the money
questions.why: About a 10% chance it ends in the money. Some traders read delta that way. It's cheap because it needs a strong move to be worth anything at expiry.
questions.lesson_line: A low-delta option is cheap because it probably won't pay. Price the odds, not the ticket.

wrong.It gains $10 for each $1 the stock rises: Delta is per dollar of stock. A 0.10 delta means about a dime per $1, not $10.
wrong.It loses 10% of its value each day: That's theta's job, and theta is quoted in dollars, not percent.
wrong.It is 10% out of the money: Delta isn't the distance to the strike. It's price sensitivity, read here as rough odds.

questions.story: You own 100 shares of a leading stock you expect to run for months. A friend says to sell covered calls for income.
questions.q: What's the catch for your plan?
choices: Your upside is capped at the strike
You lose the premium if it falls
questions.answer: Your upside is capped at the strike
questions.why: Your upside is capped at the strike. While the call is open, you give up most of the gains above it. A rally can get your shares called away.
questions.lesson_line: Don't sell calls on a stock you want to hold for the big move.

wrong.Your downside risk becomes unlimited: The short call doesn't add downside risk. The stock's own risk is what it was.
wrong.You must buy 100 more shares: Your 100 shares already cover one call. There's nothing more to buy.
wrong.You lose the premium if it falls: You keep the premium whatever the stock does. The buyer paid it to you.

questions.q: When you buy a call, you can lose more than the premium you paid.
questions.why: False. An option buyer can't lose more than the price paid. The worst case is holding to expiration with the stock below the strike.
questions.lesson_line: Buying options caps the loss at the premium. Size that premium as your full risk, because all of it can go.

questions.q: Standard monthly equity options generally have their last trading day on the third Friday of the month.
questions.why: True. If that Friday is an exchange holiday, it moves to the Thursday before. Many products also have weekly expirations, so check each contract.
questions.lesson_line: Read the expiration date on every contract. Not every option expires on the third Friday.

conflicts: Expiration day: the SEC's options bulletin (updated July 16, 2026) still says the expiration date is 'generally the Saturday after the third Friday'. OIC's current glossary (Expiration Friday) and Options Basics say standard equity options generally have their last trading day, and usually expire, on the third Friday. q66 follows OIC and is phrased as the last trading day; no question uses the SEC's Saturday line.

European-style wording differs: OIC's glossary and FINRA say 'only during a specified period just prior to expiration'; OIC's FAQ: Basics says 'only on its expiration date'; OIC's FAQ: Options Exercise says the last trading day. q20 and q55 say 'only at expiration' / 'at or just before expiration', which all three support, and q55 keys on OIC's line that a European-style position can still be closed in the market any day.

Exercise statistics disagree across OIC's own FAQs ('more than 72%' closed before expiration, 'about 70%' sold to close, 'about 7%' exercised; FINRA also says about 7%). No question keys any percentage; q19's lesson avoids 'most holders sell'.

Exercise by exception: OCC's threshold is $.01 in the money (OIC FAQs), but OIC says 'your firm may have a different threshold', and some brokers act on expiring positions under their own risk rules. q56 asks only what happens 'under OCC's standard procedure' and its why and lesson tell the member to give the broker instructions.

Delta as probability is a trader's convention, not a definition: OIC says 'Some traders view Delta as a percentage probability'. q63 asks it as 'read as a rough probability'; q21 lists it as how some traders read delta.

Expected move: no single official definition. OIC (Rule of 16 takeaways) says an implied-volatility move 'describes magnitude of expected movement, not direction'; Schwab's Market Maker Move page says the figure guarantees no size and no direction. q61 keys only on those shared points and uses the generic phrase 'expected move', not a platform's indicator name.

Iron condor naming: OIC files the credit iron condor as 'Short Condor (Iron Condor)' and calls the iron butterfly the 'Short Iron Butterfly'. Questions use the common names (iron condor, iron butterfly) for the credit versions, matching the Journal's labels, and cite the OIC pages for the structure and the max loss.

Journal labels vs textbook names: the Journal's 'Put Credit Spread' and 'Call Credit Spread' are OIC's bull put spread and bear call spread (OIC's own page titles carry both names, and its glossary lists both as credit spreads). q36 and q49 teach that mapping.

Seen and NOT used: OIC's glossary entry on strike price intervals gives old standard increments while saying many stocks are exempt; OIC's FAQ gives an exercise cut-off of 4:30 p.m. CT for exchanges (time-sensitive, broker cut-offs are earlier); FINRA's assignment page says SPX options are 'tied to S&P 500 futures contracts' (SPX options are on the index); OIC's open interest article has a typo in its third example (Trader A's position 'transferred to Trader B' where it means C). No fact or question relies on these; q59 uses only the article's summary rules.

Investopedia's options-chain page says higher volume and open interest mean options 'are more easily traded and have tighter bid-ask spreads'; OIC's FAQ calls equating volume and open interest with liquidity 'a common misconception' and points to the quoted market and its size. q17 and q58 stay on what open interest counts; q48 cites the Investopedia page only for what a chain lists.
Taxes: OIC's General Information FAQ mentions the wash-sale rule. Out of scope by the owner's ruling (ask a tax professional); nothing here touches it.
